query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy, introducing interstitial oxygen (as in the O-2 HEA variant) can enhance the glass-forming ability by creating ordered oxygen complexes that increase local chemical disorder and disrupt crystal nucleation during cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy prepared by arc-melting and drop-casting (as in the base HEA formulation)
generation.intervention: Interstitial oxygen doping to form an oxygen-doped HEA (similar to the O-2 HEA) at a concentration that promotes the formation of ordered oxygen complexes
generation.conditions: Processing conditions similar to the reported arc-melting and water-cooled drop-casting technique, with rapid cooling such that any increase in atomic disorder due to oxygen can influence crystallization kinetics
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) among the constituent atoms
generation.mechanism: Oxygen doping is expected to enhance local chemical disorder and increase atomic size mismatches. The OOCs, by disrupting the short-range ordering typical of crystalline phases, would slow down atomic mobility and impede nucleation, thus lowering the critical cooling rate required to form an amorphous (glass) structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped base HEA, the oxygen-doped HEA should exhibit a lower critical cooling rate and increased glass-forming ability, with evidence of an amorphous structure or enhanced glass stability in thermal analyses.
generation.baseline: The base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA prepared without interstitial oxygen doping, which is expected to crystallize more readily under similar cooling conditions.
generation.boundary: The enhancement in glass-forming ability is likely limited to oxygen concentrations that promote OOC formation without causing detrimental phase segregation or embrittlement. Excess oxygen might instead induce unwanted secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence linking oxygen doping to enhanced glass-forming ability in these HEAs is limited; the hypothesis extrapolates from observed effects of oxygen on damping and mechanical properties, so further targeted experiments are needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs: one with controlled oxygen doping (targeting concentrations similar to the reported O-2 HEA) and one without doping. Subject both sets to identical rapid quenching procedures. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze the phases and detect any amorphous content.
measurements: XRD patterns to check for the presence or absence of sharp crystalline peaks
DSC measurements to identify the glass transition temperature and crystallization onset
TEM micrographs to observe the nanostructure and assess any amorphous regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped sample does not show a significant reduction in the critical cooling rate for glass formation (i.e., no evidence of enhanced amorphous content or improved glass stability compared to the undoped baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
